title: Foreword: The Challenge of the AI Era and the Need for Hwajaeng
content:
As humanity enters the AI era, it faces a crisis on two fronts. Internally, it confronts the danger of mass layoffs; externally—as seen in the U.S.–Iran war—it faces a crisis in which war situations that, before the AI era, had remained mere possibilities are now being pushed to their extreme. Accordingly, the re-establishment of humanity's identity, together with mutual flourishing and connection achieved through *hwajaeng* (和諍, the harmonization of disputes), has become an essential task for human survival.

Just as the Eastern proverb says, "Even if the sky falls, there is a hole through which to rise," the West has Gödel's incompleteness theorems. This is the theorem that, however perfect a logic may be—like that of AI—there can never be a logic without gaps (Kim Sang-il, 2003). That humanity has an answer is certain; the key now is to find the method.

The re-establishment of human identity can be found in the method of correlative thinking that sees the whole first. The mass layoffs that AI has brought about today are, in many cases, mistaken decisions biased toward the analytic method that sees the part before the whole. Humanity's traditional methods of correlative thinking, which see the whole before the part—for example, the Eastern modes of multidimensionality/transcendence, circulation, empathy, and convergence—can serve as methodological alternatives that resolve the errors of AI's analytic thinking, which fails to survey the connected whole: errors such as confirmation bias and cognitive dissonance. It is the same principle as how, looking down at a mountain from its summit, one easily discovers what could never be seen from below. Moreover, the advance of artificial intelligence goes beyond mere technological innovation; it amplifies conflicts between nations, between groups, and between classes, and gives birth to new forms of opposition. If multidimensionality/transcendence, circulation, empathy, and convergence are theories concerning the correlative thinking of the individual, then *hwajaeng*, developed within Buddhism, may be called the application of correlative thinking in relation to the community.

*Hwajaeng* has itself developed through subdivision within Buddhism according to circumstance. It began from a binary (二項) relation between arising-and-ceasing (生滅, *saengmyeol*) and suchness (眞如, *jinyeo*); later, with the emergence of Consciousness-Only thought (唯識, *yusik*), it became a relation of the Three Natures (三性), that is, a ternary (三項) relation; and later still, with the appearance of Pure Land Buddhism (淨土宗) and the like, it developed into a quaternary (四項) relation. The problems facing humanity today likewise arise, in the end, from the collision of four economic theories that can be resolved through the four-term relation of *hwajaeng*. This book, in Part I (Theory), presents the four modes of correlative thinking—multidimensionality (立體), circulation (循環), empathy (共感), and convergence (融合)—and, in Part II (Application), links these to the four-gate (四門) structure of Wonhyo's *hwajaeng* theory in order to present a method for a mutually flourishing, connected economy.

*April 2026, at the foot of Mount Wangbang*
